newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives swept away in Labour tidal wave.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives swept away in Labour tidal wave.

text.p: A tidal wave of support swept Tony Blair's new-look Labour Party back to power on Friday for the first time since 1979 as Britain rose up to inflict a humiliating defeat on John Major's Conservatives.
The defeat was on a scale unseen for 165 years with six cabinet ministers, including Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, losing their seats.
Labour clinched its biggest victory shortly after 0200 GMT when it won its 330th seat in the 659-seat parliament.
Prime Minister John Major, re-elected in his safe Huntingdon constituency, was grim as he stared out on a rout that opinion polls had flagged but few politicians had thought possible.

"Tonight we have been comprehensively defeated," Major said. His party will probably lose half its seats by the time the final result is announced later on Friday and will have to oppose a Labour Party with a record majority of about 185.
"I telephoned Mr Blair an hour ago to congratulate him on his success... and to wish him every good fortune in the great responsibility he will have in the years that lie ahead," Major said.
His Downing Street office said he would hand in his resignation to Queen Elizabeth, the head of state, at 1030 GMT.

Blair, who has dumped Labour's left-wing policies to reach out to the middle class voters who decide British elections. choked back tears as he made an acceptance speech in his Sedgefield seat in north-east England.
"You have put your trust in me and I intend to repay that trust. I will not let you down," said Blair, who at 43 will be Britain's youngest prime minister this century.
"We are a great country, the British people are a great people. There is no greater honour than to serve them, and serve them we will."

Major's appeal to voters, after 18 years of Conservative rule, was "better the devil you know than the devil you don't". But infighting over ties with Europe, broken promises over tax and allegations of sleaze in the ruling party doomed him to defeat.
The landslide was a ringing endorsement for Blair's crusade, since he became Labour leader in 1994, to dump the socialist baggage that led it to four successive election defeats.
Blair has promised change -- but not too much change -- with a number of limited but specific commitments that some commentators have dubbed Conservatism with a human face.

Hundreds of cheering Labour supporters toasted their landslide with champagne at the Royal Festival Hall on the banks of the River Thames as the party's campaign anthem "Things Can Only Get Better" rang out.

Conservatives were devastated by the rout, which left the party without any members of parliament in Scotland and vast swathes of south-west England, where the minority Liberal Democrats inflicted most damage.
"It is a dark night for the Conservative party," Home Secretary Michael Howard, the interior minister, said.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said the results were "shattering". Portillo, who would have been a leading right-wing candidate in any future leadership contest, said the evening had been "truly terrible".
Although senior Conservatives appealed for the party to pull together in the hour of defeat, others wasted no time drawing their knives.
Nicholas Winterton, a Euro-sceptic opposed to closer ties with Brussels, blamed finance minister Kenneth Clarke for refusing to rule out joining the European Union's planned single currency one day.
"He will be remembered, even reviled in history for his actions," Winterton said.
But the Tory Reform Group on the left wing of the party blamed the "rank treachery" of right-wingers, who it said had "run a vile campaign of hatred against John Major and his administration".
The recriminations laid bare the deep divisions over Europe that dogged Major's 6-1/2 years as prime minister.
Meanwhile the centre-left Liberal Democrats, Britain's third party, were on the brink of the great breakthrough promised by party leader Paddy Ashdown.
The BBC projected the Lib Dems, which promised to raise taxes to improve Britain's schools, could at least double the 20 seats they won at the 1992 election.
"I think the mood of the country was for a change after 18 years in power," Sir David Steel, former Lib-Dem leader, said.

Another notable result was BBC war reporter Martin Bell's easy victory in the northwest seat of Tatton against former Conservative minister Neil Hamilton, whose failure to shake off allegations of sleaze prompted Bell to stand as an independent.
